concepts.topicTitle: Ideas about atoms before the models
concepts.label: Ancient Roots of the Atom: Kanada and Democritus
concepts.cardText: More than 2,000 years ago, thinkers in ancient India and ancient Greece asked what everything is made of. Acharya Kanada suggested that if matter (dravya) is divided repeatedly you reach the smallest particles that can no longer be divided, which he called parmanus; his ideas are recorded in the Sanskrit text Vaisesika Sutras. A parmanu is infinitely small and cannot be perceived by the senses; combinations form dyads (groups of two) and triads (groups of three), and out of these the whole material universe is created, though the description does not specify the proportions in which parmanus combine. The Greek philosophers Leucippus and Democritus proposed a similar idea and called the indivisible particles atomos, meaning indivisible. The concept of an atom originated as an imaginary idea rather than from experimental observations.

concepts.topicTitle: Ideas about atoms before the models
concepts.label: Dalton's Atomic Theory
concepts.cardText: In 1808 John Dalton proposed his atomic theory, which was based on the scientific experiments of that time. He proposed that all matter is composed of indivisible particles called atoms, the fundamental building blocks of matter that cannot be broken down into smaller parts. Dalton's atomic theory was the first scientific description of how matter is made and the starting point for the current understanding of atomic structure. It raised new questions: what are atoms made up of, what would atoms look like if we could see them, and what makes the atoms of one element different from the atoms of another. Early atomic models were later changed and improved as new evidence came to light; although they are not fully correct they are important because they show how science moves forward one step at a time, driven by curiosity, questioning and experimentation.

concepts.label: Radioactivity and the Discovery of the Electron
concepts.cardText: Until the late 19th century atoms were thought to be the smallest, indivisible units of matter. But scientists discovered that certain elements emit invisible energy and particles called radiation, a phenomenon known as radioactivity, which showed that atoms must be composed of smaller particles. In 1897 J. J. Thomson studied the conduction of electric current through gases at very low pressure, using a glass tube with two electrodes and a high voltage. He observed rays moving from the cathode (negative electrode) to the anode (positive electrode), called cathode rays. By studying these rays in electric and magnetic fields he concluded that they are streams of negatively charged particles with a much smaller mass than atoms; these particles, later called electrons, were emitted from atoms, so atoms are composed of smaller subatomic components. The nature of cathode rays was independent of the cathode material and the gas in the tube, which showed that electrons are a fundamental component of all atoms, present in every element.

concepts.label: Thomson's Plum Pudding Model
concepts.cardText: When J. J. Thomson discovered tiny negatively charged particles called electrons he faced a puzzle: atoms are neutral, so where is the positive charge? To solve this, Thomson proposed the atom to be a sphere of positive charge with electrons distributed throughout it. This model was compared to a pudding with plums embedded in it, called the plum pudding model, or to a watermelon, where the red pulp represents the positively charged matter and the seeds represent electrons distributed throughout the atom. This simple picture, though later replaced, was the first genuine attempt to describe how the atom's positive and negative charges stay balanced. Atoms do not show any colour; the colours in diagrams are only illustrative. Thomson received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906 for his studies of the electrical conductivity of gases.

concepts.label: The Gold Foil Experiment
concepts.cardText: In 1911 Geiger and Marsden, working under Ernest Rutherford, tested Thomson's model with the gold foil experiment. They aimed a narrow beam of alpha particles, tiny positively charged particles emitted from certain radioactive elements, at an extremely thin sheet of gold foil. According to Thomson's model the positive charge was spread out evenly, so they expected the alpha particles to pass straight through or be deflected only slightly. To their surprise, most particles passed through undeflected, some were sharply deflected and a few even bounced back; this deflection from the straight path is called scattering, so the experiment is also called the alpha-ray scattering experiment. Thomson's model failed to explain the results, particularly the deflection of some alpha particles through large angles while most passed undeflected.

concepts.label: Rutherford's Nuclear (Planetary) Model
concepts.cardText: From the gold foil experiment Rutherford concluded that the positive charge of an atom is not spread throughout but is concentrated in an extremely small region called the nucleus. He proposed that most of an atom is empty space, as most alpha particles passed through the foil without any deflection; the nucleus is dense and contains all the positive charge and most of the mass of an atom; and the electrons revolve around the nucleus somewhat like planets orbiting the Sun, so this is called the planetary model of the atom. Rutherford found that the nucleus is extremely small, about one lakh times smaller than the atom. If an atom were the size of a cricket ground of about 100 m across, the nucleus would be a tiny black pepper grain of a few mm at the centre.

concepts.label: Limitation of Rutherford's Model and the Discovery of the Proton
concepts.cardText: Rutherford's model was better than Thomson's in explaining the gold foil results, but it could not explain the stability of the atom. A particle moving in a circular path is constantly changing direction, which means it is accelerating. If a negatively charged electron keeps accelerating around the nucleus it should lose energy, spiral inward and eventually fall into the positively charged nucleus; atoms would collapse and not exist, but in reality atoms are stable. So the model was not completely correct and a new explanation was needed. Rutherford also discovered and named the proton: the nucleus carries positive charge which comes from particles called protons, which are much heavier than electrons and possess a charge equal and opposite to that of electrons. For an atom to be electrically neutral the number of protons equals the number of electrons: a helium atom has 2 protons and 2 electrons, and a sodium atom has 11 and 11. All atoms are electrically neutral.

concepts.label: Bohr's Model of the Atom
concepts.cardText: To explain why atoms are stable, Niels Bohr proposed a new model in 1913. According to Bohr, electrons do not move randomly around the nucleus but follow fixed circular paths called stationary states, orbits or shells. In each shell an electron has a definite amount of energy, so the shells are also called energy levels, named K, L, M, N or n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Electrons can revolve only in these allowed shells and not in between, and while moving in a fixed shell an electron does not lose energy. The first level K (n = 1) is closest to the nucleus and has the least energy, and the energy increases as we move away from the nucleus. An electron can move to another shell by absorbing or releasing a fixed amount of energy equal to the difference between the energies of the two levels, and each shell can hold only a certain number of electrons. Bohr explained stability by introducing stationary states as a postulate: in a stationary state the energy of an electron remains constant even though it moves around the nucleus. Even Bohr's model was later found to have limitations and the quantum mechanical model was proposed.

concepts.topicTitle: The neutron and the mass of an atom
concepts.label: Discovery of the Neutron
concepts.cardText: Rutherford's model showed that most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus, since the electrons are so light their mass can be ignored. But something puzzling appeared in the early 20th century: a hydrogen atom has one proton and a helium atom has two protons, yet the mass of a helium atom is about four times that of a hydrogen atom, not double. In 1932 James Chadwick, a student of Rutherford, solved this by discovering a new subatomic particle with a mass nearly equal to that of a proton but no electrical charge. This neutral particle was named the neutron, usually represented by the symbol n. Neutrons are found in the nucleus of all atoms except hydrogen. The mass of an atom comes mainly from its protons and neutrons packed tightly in the nucleus, which explains why atoms are heavier than the mass of their total number of protons.

concepts.topicTitle: The neutron and the mass of an atom
concepts.label: Why Heavier Atoms Need More Neutrons
concepts.cardText: Lighter atoms often have an equal number of protons and neutrons, like carbon with six each or oxygen with eight each. But as atoms get heavier their nuclei have many more neutrons than protons: iron has 26 protons and 30 neutrons, and uranium has 92 protons and 146 neutrons. Every proton inside the nucleus repels every other proton because they all carry positive charge. Neutrons, being neutral, help reduce this repulsion by increasing the distance between protons and by strengthening the nuclear force that binds all particles together. So heavier atoms need many more neutrons to hold everything in the nucleus tightly bound.

concepts.topicTitle: Elements: symbols, atomic number and mass number
concepts.label: Symbols of Elements
concepts.cardText: By 1869 scientists knew about 69 elements, and today about 118 unique chemical elements are known, some artificially made. John Dalton realised the need for a standard way to represent elements and in 1803 introduced the first pictorial symbols. In 1813 Berzelius suggested that symbols should be derived from the Latin names of elements, which gave alphabetic chemical symbols. Today the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) approves the names and symbols of elements. Many symbols are the first letter or the first two letters of the name. The first letter is always a capital and the second letter, if any, a small letter: hydrogen H, aluminium Al (not AL), cobalt Co (not CO). Some symbols use the first letter and a letter other than the second, such as chlorine Cl and zinc Zn. Some come from Latin, Greek or German names: iron Fe (ferrum), mercury Hg (hydrargyros) and tungsten W (wolfram). Scientists use these symbols because they are internationally recognised and allow communication regardless of language barriers.

concepts.topicTitle: Elements: symbols, atomic number and mass number
concepts.label: Atomic Number
concepts.cardText: The atoms of an element are all alike but different from the atoms of other elements; they differ in the number of electrons and protons in them. The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom of an element is known as its atomic number, designated by the symbol Z. This number determines the identity of an element and its chemical behaviour. Since the atom as a whole is neutral, the number of protons equals the number of electrons orbiting the nucleus. Hydrogen has one proton and one electron, so its atomic number is 1; helium, with atomic number 2, has 2 protons and 2 electrons.

concepts.topicTitle: Elements: symbols, atomic number and mass number
concepts.label: Mass Number and Nucleons
concepts.cardText: The total number of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus of an atom is called its mass number, denoted by A, and the protons and neutrons in the nucleus are called nucleons. Mass number equals the number of protons plus the number of neutrons. Since the mass of a neutron is roughly equal to that of a proton, the mass of a helium atom can be accounted for by two protons and two neutrons. The electron has almost negligible mass in comparison, so it can be ignored in calculations. In the standard notation the symbol, the atomic number Z and the mass number A are written together; for example carbon has symbol C, atomic number 6 and mass number 12.

concepts.label: Distribution of Electrons in Shells
concepts.cardText: Bohr and Bury suggested rules for filling electrons. The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by 2n squared, where n is the number of the shell: the K shell (n = 1) holds 2 electrons, the L shell (n = 2) holds 8 and the M shell (n = 3) holds 18. The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the outermost shell is 8, with the first shell holding a maximum of two. Electrons are filled in a stepwise manner, starting from the shell closest to the nucleus and moving outward in the order K, L, M, N; the L shell is filled only after the K shell is complete, and so on. Hydrogen's only electron is in the K shell, and helium's two electrons also fill the K shell. The distribution of electrons among the shells is known as the electronic configuration of the atom.

concepts.label: Valency, Octet and the Valence Shell
concepts.cardText: The number of atoms of hydrogen or chlorine with which one atom of an element can combine to form a compound is called its combining capacity, since both have a combining capacity of one; oxygen in water (H2O) combines with two hydrogen atoms so its combining capacity is two. The outermost shell containing electrons is the valence shell and its electrons are valence electrons. If the outermost shell has 8 electrons it is called an octet. Elements with a complete octet, or 2 electrons in the case of helium, in their valence shell are largely unreactive and more stable, while atoms with incomplete valence shells are usually more reactive and lose, gain or share electrons to complete their octet. The number of electrons gained, lost or shared to complete the octet is the valency of the element. With fewer than four valence electrons an element tends to lose electrons, and with more than four it tends to gain electrons. Sodium (2, 8, 1) loses one electron, so its valency is 1; oxygen (2, 6) gains two, so its valency is 2; carbon (2, 4) shares four, so its valency is 4.

concepts.topicTitle: Isotopes, isobars and average atomic mass
concepts.label: Isotopes
concepts.cardText: Dalton proposed that all atoms of an element are identical with the same mass, but scientists later discovered atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons (the same atomic number) yet different numbers of neutrons, and so different mass numbers. These atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers are called isotopes. Naturally occurring hydrogen is a mixture of three isotopes, protium, deuterium and tritium; all contain one proton, deuterium contains one neutron and tritium contains two neutrons. Carbon likewise has three isotopes, each with six protons and six electrons but a different number of neutrons. The chemical properties of isotopes are similar because they have the same number of electrons and the same electronic configuration, and chemical properties depend mainly on the number of valence electrons; they differ in physical properties such as boiling and melting points. Atomic masses are measured in the unified atomic mass unit (u).

concepts.label: Applications of Isotopes
concepts.cardText: Some isotopes have special properties useful in various fields. An isotope of uranium is used as a fuel in a nuclear reactor to generate electricity in a nuclear power plant. An isotope of carbon is used in archaeology and geology to determine the age of ancient fossils and artefacts.

concepts.topicTitle: Isotopes, isobars and average atomic mass
concepts.label: Average Atomic Mass
concepts.cardText: Chlorine occurs in nature as two isotopes, one of mass 35 u and the other of mass 37 u, in the ratio 3:1. The simple arithmetic mean of 35 and 37 is 36 u, but this does not accurately reflect nature, since isotopes do not occur in equal ratios; the more common isotope, chlorine-35, makes up about 75% and chlorine-37 about 25%. The accurate value is the weighted average atomic mass, calculated by multiplying the mass of each isotope by its percent relative abundance and adding the values, which gives about 35.5 u. This does not mean that any one atom of chlorine has a fractional mass of 35.5 u: in 1 million chlorine atoms about 7.5 lakh have mass 35 u and 2.5 lakh have mass 37 u. The simple average ignores abundance, whereas the weighted average accurately reflects the mass of the element as it occurs in nature.

concepts.topicTitle: Isotopes, isobars and average atomic mass
concepts.label: Isobars and Beyond Bohr's Model
concepts.cardText: Calcium (atomic number 20), potassium (19) and argon (18) have different numbers of protons, yet each has a mass number of 40, so the total number of nucleons in their atoms is the same even though they are different elements. When atoms of different elements have the same mass number but different atomic numbers, they are called isobars. The exploration of the structure of the atom is still continuing: scientists later discovered that even Bohr's model was not entirely correct. Electrons do not follow well-defined paths like the fixed Bohr orbits; today we understand that they exist as electron clouds around the nucleus, and we can predict regions where they are most likely to be, not exactly where they are.
